name: Luvian
confidence_why: Melchert 2004 writes that the placement of the Luvian accent can be inferred only in a limited way and at a high risk of circularity, Yakubovich 2013 states outright that the synchronic character of Luwian stress is unclear, and Rieken 2017 recovers accent position only word by word from plene spellings and etymology, so no source proposes a placement rule.
catalog_citation: Melchert, H. Craig. 2004. Luvian. In Roger D. Woodard (ed.), The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages, 576-584. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. (Reprinted 2008 in R. D. Woodard (ed.), The Ancient Languages of Asia Minor, 31-39 = Glottolog ref 104631.) Author's self-archived scan (the Internet Archive copy).
catalog_locator: p. 580, sec. 3.2 Vowels (300-dpi render, crop viewed)
catalog_quote: Luvian has only three vowels, /a/, /i/, and /u/, in contrasting short and long varieties. While there are some underlying long vowels, most phonetic length is due to synchronic rules which lengthen underlying short vowels under the accent: contrast sentence-initial conjunction pā < /pá/ versus enclitic -pa < /-pa/, or adverb ānnan "under" < /ánnan/ versus annān pātanza "under the feet" < /annán/ with accent shift in a prepositional phrase (see Melchert 1994a:247 for further discussion). ... Certain facts about the placement of the accent may be inferred from the prehistoric and synchronic rules cited in the preceding two paragraphs, but the evidence is limited, and the risk of circularity of argument is high.
world_status: statement found in an open source

(Reprinted 2008 in R. D. Woodard (ed.), The Ancient Languages of Asia Minor, 31-39 — the Glottolog-listed item 104631.)
new_statements.locator: p. 580, section 3.2 Vowels (p. 31 of the 64-page author scan)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: is a 64-page scan-only scan (the PDF's metadata); the 300-dpi render scanned/ carries the running header "580 The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages" (cropped and viewed), so p. 31 = book p. 580 as stated. I viewed scanned/ myself: sec. 3.2 Vowels reads exactly as quoted, including the diacritics the scanned drops (pā < /pá/ vs -pa < /-pa/; ānnan "under" < /ánnan/ vs annān pātanza "under the feet" < /annán/; "see Melchert 1994a:247"), and the second paragraph "Certain facts about the placement of the accent may be inferred from the prehistoric and synchronic rules cited in the preceding two paragraphs, but the evidence is limited, and the risk of circularit…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The source gives no placement rule: the accent of this extinct language is known only indirectly, through accent-conditioned vowel lengthening reflected in cuneiform plene spellings (accented short vowels in open syllables and initial position lengthen; unaccented vowels, e.g. enclitics, do not) and through prehistoric sound changes. Where inferable it is a free/mobile inherited (Indo-European-type) accent that can differ between homophonous forms (/pá/ vs. enclitic /-pa/) and shift within a phrase (/ánnan/ vs. /annán/ in annān pātanza), i.e. not fixed to any syllable. Yakubovich 2013:115 says the same in Russian: the synchronic nature of Luwian stress is unclear; only stressed word forms vs. enclitics can be told apart.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent shift onto the final syllable of the adverb in a prepositional phrase (ānnan 'under' /ánnan/ vs. annān pātanza 'under the feet' /annán/); enclitics are unaccented (-pa vs. pā). Rieken 2017:24 adds that Čop's Rule presupposes first-syllable stress in mallī(t)- 'honey', while the place of stress in many lexemes remains uncertain (Rieken 2017:27; Yakubovich 2008:394 fn. 10 for the same caveat in Hittite).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent inferred from orthography (plene writing) of a dead language attested 16th-13th c. BCE; the word/phrase contrast is explicit (accent shift in a prepositional phrase). Melchert's phonology is stated to be based primarily on Cuneiform Luvian data, though the chapter covers both Cuneiform and Hieroglyphic Luvian.
new_statements.identity_note: Melchert 2004 covers 'Luvian' as one language written in two scripts and states (p. 579) that its phonological analysis is based primarily on Cuneiform Luvian data, so the accent statement applies to cune1239; Hieroglyphic Luwian is a separate Glottolog entry (Hieroglyphic Luwian, iso hlu; code not verified here). Yakubovich 2013 likewise treats Luwian as a whole, with the cuneiform corpus representing the Kizzuwatna ritual koine and 'Empire Luwian' words in Hittite texts. Rieken 2017 is specifically on Cuneiform Luwian.

sources.note: The chapter states no placement rule: the author says only that accent placement 'may be inferred' partly from the vowel-lengthening and prehistoric rules, 'but the evidence is limited, and the risk of circularity of argument is high' (p. 580). What it does state: (i) accent lengthens underlying short vowels (phonetic length is mostly accent-driven); (ii) accent position is contrastive/mobile, shown by pá (sentence-initial conjunction) vs unaccented enclitic -pa and by ánnan 'under' vs annán pátanza 'under the feet', described as 'accent shift in a prepositional phrase'; (iii) enclitics attach

sources.citation: Vertegaal, Alexander J. J. 2020. Voices in Stone: Studies in Luwian Historical Phonology. PhD dissertation, Leiden University (defended 4 June 2020; promotor A. M. Lubotsky, co-promotor A. Kloekhorst; committee incl. E. Rieken, I.-X. Adiego). LOT Dissertation Series 564. Amsterdam: LOT. xxii+219 pp. ISBN 978-94-6093-349-3.
sources.note: No tone posited; the Luwian/Proto-Anatolian accent is treated as a stress accent ('at least a very strong stress component'), diagnosed by accent-conditioned vowel and consonant lengthening; Čop's Law and open-syllable lengthening made every accented syllable heavy, so vowel length, consonant length and syllable weight became dependent on the place of the stress; accent position is reconstructed word by word from plene spelling/gemination and etymology (radical vs. suffixal accent, ch. 2), no synchronic placement rule.

tone.quote: Note that the lengthening effects mentioned here make it very likely that the Proto-Anatolian accent had at least a very strong stress component (Melchert 1994a: 47). [...] The Luwian state of affairs, in which all accented syllables are heavy, has a great number of parallels among the world’s languages (Gordon 1999: 23–31), and seems to be a stable point of convergence of stress-based phonological systems. [...] leading to the situation in Proto-Luwic where syllable weight, vowel length and consonantal length became dependent on the place of the stress accent and lost much of their contrastive value to a significant degree.
